title: May Day
hookLine: many countries honor workers on 1 May or in early September

cards: A cup of morning coffee passes through more hands than anyone drinking it will ever meet. Someone picked the beans. Someone drove the truck.
Someone stocked the shelf, someone fixed the pipe that brings the water, someone cleaned the floor of the shop before it opened. Their faces aren't on the cup, and their names aren't on the receipt.
In a number of countries, one day a year tries to fix that. In some it falls on the first of May. In the United States and Canada, it's Labor Day, in early September.

teach.b: First, the day itself. Workers' days are marked in different ways: parades, speeches, a day off, a cookout at the end of summer. Some are political, some just restful.
The idea underneath is simple: the people who do the work should be seen. Second, an old law about wages. The book of Leviticus sets a rule about hired workers.

In the King James words: "the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning." Pay the day laborer the same day. Deuteronomy explains why: he is poor, and he has set his heart on it.
A day's wage held back overnight is a family's dinner held back. Third, a teaching in Islam.
A hadith, a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, reported in Ibn Majah, says, in paraphrase: give the worker his wages before his sweat dries. Not next month. Not after the paperwork.
Two traditions, the same urgency about the person who did the work. Fourth, a saint in an apron.

The Catholic Church keeps the first of May as a feast of Saint Joseph the Worker, the carpenter of Nazareth. So on the same day some streets fill with banners, some churches remember a man with sawdust on his sleeves.
What these share is a turn of attention. The finished thing, the coffee, the clean floor, the working pipe, is easy to see. The hands that made it are easy to miss.
A workers' day is a day for looking past the thing to the hands.

how: On workers' days, people take part in parades and gatherings, take a day off, or simply rest; some Catholics keep 1 May as the feast of Saint Joseph the Worker.

games.q: you hired someone for a day's work. it's evening, and you're tired. by Leviticus, when do you pay?
o: at the end of the week.
games.why: Leviticus says the wages shall not wait all night until the morning, and Deuteronomy adds why: the worker is poor and is counting on it.

practice: Hold in mind one ordinary thing you've used today, a cup, a light switch, a bus seat, and trace it backward one pair of hands at a time: who made it, who moved it, who kept it working, who cleaned up after.
You won't know their names; just let them be there, one after another. If you pray, you can hold them in your own tradition's words.
